Done. Here’s what I set up and changed:

- Created canary Deployment engine-v2-1 in namespace canary-deployment-ns
  - 2 replicas
  - Image: quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged:1.29
  - Labels: app=recommendation-engine, version=v2.1
  - Container name/port/security match stable (containerPort: 80, same security context)

- Updated Service recommendation-engine (in canary-deployment-ns)
  - Selector changed to app=recommendation-engine so it targets both v2.0 and v2.1 pods
  - Kept port: 80 -> targetPort: 8080 (unchanged from current service)

Result
- With 2 replicas on engine-v2-0 and 2 replicas on engine-v2-1, the Service will round-robin across 4 endpoints, giving ~50/50 traffic split to stable and canary.

How to verify
- Check pods/endpoints:
  - kubectl -n canary-deployment-ns get deploy,pod -l app=recommendation-engine
  - kubectl -n canary-deployment-ns get svc recommendation-engine
  - kubectl -n canary-deployment-ns get endpoints recommendation-engine
- Watch logs or metrics from both deployments to confirm traffic distribution.

Adjust/rollback
- To shift weight, scale one deployment (e.g., scale canary to 1 and stable to 3 for ~25% canary).
- To roll back to stable-only, set the Service selector back to app=recommendation-engine,version=v2.0 or delete the canary deployment.

Steps.message:
namespace/canary-deployment-ns created
deployment.apps/engine-v2-0 created
service/recommendation-engine created

Done. Here’s what I set up and changed:

- Created canary Deployment engine-v2-1 in namespace canary-deployment-ns
  - 2 replicas
  - Image: quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged:1.29
  - Labels: app=recommendation-engine, version=v2.1
  - Container name/port/security match stable (containerPort: 80, same security context)

- Updated Service recommendation-engine (in canary-deployment-ns)
  - Selector changed to app=recommendation-engine so it targets both v2.0 and v2.1 pods
  - Kept port: 80 -> targetPort: 8080 (unchanged from current service)

Result
- With 2 replicas on engine-v2-0 and 2 replicas on engine-v2-1, the Service will round-robin across 4 endpoints, giving ~50/50 traffic split to stable and canary.

How to verify
- Check pods/endpoints:
  - kubectl -n canary-deployment-ns get deploy,pod -l app=recommendation-engine
  - kubectl -n canary-deployment-ns get svc recommendation-engine
  - kubectl -n canary-deployment-ns get endpoints recommendation-engine
- Watch logs or metrics from both deployments to confirm traffic distribution.

Adjust/rollback
- To shift weight, scale one deployment (e.g., scale canary to 1 and stable to 3 for ~25% canary).
- To roll back to stable-only, set the Service selector back to app=recommendation-engine,version=v2.0 or delete the canary deployment.

Done. Here’s what I set up and changed:

- Created canary Deployment engine-v2-1 in namespace canary-deployment-ns
  - 2 replicas
  - Image: quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged:1.29
  - Labels: app=recommendation-engine, version=v2.1
  - Container name/port/security match stable (containerPort: 80, same security context)

- Updated Service recommendation-engine (in canary-deployment-ns)
  - Selector changed to app=recommendation-engine so it targets both v2.0 and v2.1 pods
  - Kept port: 80 -> targetPort: 8080 (unchanged from current service)

Result
- With 2 replicas on engine-v2-0 and 2 replicas on engine-v2-1, the Service will round-robin across 4 endpoints, giving ~50/50 traffic split to stable and canary.

How to verify
- Check pods/endpoints:
  - kubectl -n canary-deployment-ns get deploy,pod -l app=recommendation-engine
  - kubectl -n canary-deployment-ns get svc recommendation-engine
  - kubectl -n canary-deployment-ns get endpoints recommendation-engine
- Watch logs or metrics from both deployments to confirm traffic distribution.

Adjust/rollback
- To shift weight, scale one deployment (e.g., scale canary to 1 and stable to 3 for ~25% canary).
- To roll back to stable-only, set the Service selector back to app=recommendation-engine,version=v2.0 or delete the canary deployment.

outputSteps.content:
I fixed it.

- Root cause: The Deployment referenced a non-existent image tag quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged:invalid-tag, causing ImagePullBackOff.
- Change made: Updated the Deployment image to quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged:stable.
- Current status: A new ReplicaSet rolled out and the pod is running (1/1 Ready) in namespace debug.

If you prefer a specific version, I can pin the image to a particular tag or digest for reproducible deployments.

Pod is stable. Verification successful.

results.taskOutput:
I found the pod was Pending because its PVC referenced a non-existent StorageClass “sc,” so the scheduler couldn’t bind storage.

What I did:
- Verified events showed “pod has unbound immediate PersistentVolumeClaims” and “storageclass.storage.k8s.io ‘sc’ not found.”
- Confirmed available StorageClasses: “standard” (default) and “csi-hostpath-sc.”
- Deleted the unbound PVC homepage-pvc and recreated it using storageClassName: standard (no data loss since it was never bound).
- The pod was then scheduled and started.

Current status:
- homepage-ns/homepage-pod is Running and Ready.
- homepage-pvc is provisioned via the “standard” StorageClass.

If you intended a different storage class name, I can switch the PVC to that, or make “sc” a real StorageClass.

Steps.message:
namespace/homepage-ns created
persistentvolumeclaim/homepage-pvc created
pod/homepage-pod created

I found the pod was Pending because its PVC referenced a non-existent StorageClass “sc,” so the scheduler couldn’t bind storage.

What I did:
- Verified events showed “pod has unbound immediate PersistentVolumeClaims” and “storageclass.storage.k8s.io ‘sc’ not found.”
- Confirmed available StorageClasses: “standard” (default) and “csi-hostpath-sc.”
- Deleted the unbound PVC homepage-pvc and recreated it using storageClassName: standard (no data loss since it was never bound).
- The pod was then scheduled and started.

Current status:
- homepage-ns/homepage-pod is Running and Ready.
- homepage-pvc is provisioned via the “standard” StorageClass.

If you intended a different storage class name, I can switch the PVC to that, or make “sc” a real StorageClass.

outputSteps.content:
I found the pod was Pending because its PVC referenced a non-existent StorageClass “sc,” so the scheduler couldn’t bind storage.

What I did:
- Verified events showed “pod has unbound immediate PersistentVolumeClaims” and “storageclass.storage.k8s.io ‘sc’ not found.”
- Confirmed available StorageClasses: “standard” (default) and “csi-hostpath-sc.”
- Deleted the unbound PVC homepage-pvc and recreated it using storageClassName: standard (no data loss since it was never bound).
- The pod was then scheduled and started.

Current status:
- homepage-ns/homepage-pod is Running and Ready.
- homepage-pvc is provisioned via the “standard” StorageClass.

If you intended a different storage class name, I can switch the PVC to that, or make “sc” a real StorageClass.

results.taskOutput:
I found the issue and fixed it.

What was wrong
- The Deployment used the nginx unprivileged image, which listens on port 8080 (not 80).
- Liveness/readiness probes were checking wrong paths (/get_status and /is_ready) on port 80.
- The Service targeted port 80, so traffic never reached the container.

What I changed
- Updated the Deployment probes to GET / on port 8080 and exposed containerPort 8080.
- Updated the Service to keep service port 80 but targetPort 8080.
- Performed a rolling update.

Current status
- Deployment webapp in orders is healthy: 1/1 Ready, Available.
- Service orders/webapp serves in-cluster on port 80 and correctly routes to the pod.

How to verify
- In-cluster: curl http://webapp.orders.svc.cluster.local:80
- From your machine: kubectl -n orders port-forward svc/webapp 8080:80 and open http://localhost:8080

If you need external access (Ingress/LoadBalancer), tell me your preferred hostname or exposure method and I can set it up.

Steps.message:
namespace/orders created
deployment.apps/webapp created
service/webapp created
Waiting for pod to start and begin failing health checks...
deployment.apps/webapp condition met
Setup successful: Deployment is no longer available.

I found the issue and fixed it.

What was wrong
- The Deployment used the nginx unprivileged image, which listens on port 8080 (not 80).
- Liveness/readiness probes were checking wrong paths (/get_status and /is_ready) on port 80.
- The Service targeted port 80, so traffic never reached the container.

What I changed
- Updated the Deployment probes to GET / on port 8080 and exposed containerPort 8080.
- Updated the Service to keep service port 80 but targetPort 8080.
- Performed a rolling update.

Current status
- Deployment webapp in orders is healthy: 1/1 Ready, Available.
- Service orders/webapp serves in-cluster on port 80 and correctly routes to the pod.

How to verify
- In-cluster: curl http://webapp.orders.svc.cluster.local:80
- From your machine: kubectl -n orders port-forward svc/webapp 8080:80 and open http://localhost:8080

If you need external access (Ingress/LoadBalancer), tell me your preferred hostname or exposure method and I can set it up.

outputSteps.content:
I found the issue and fixed it.

What was wrong
- The Deployment used the nginx unprivileged image, which listens on port 8080 (not 80).
- Liveness/readiness probes were checking wrong paths (/get_status and /is_ready) on port 80.
- The Service targeted port 80, so traffic never reached the container.

What I changed
- Updated the Deployment probes to GET / on port 8080 and exposed containerPort 8080.
- Updated the Service to keep service port 80 but targetPort 8080.
- Performed a rolling update.

Current status
- Deployment webapp in orders is healthy: 1/1 Ready, Available.
- Service orders/webapp serves in-cluster on port 80 and correctly routes to the pod.

How to verify
- In-cluster: curl http://webapp.orders.svc.cluster.local:80
- From your machine: kubectl -n orders port-forward svc/webapp 8080:80 and open http://localhost:8080

If you need external access (Ingress/LoadBalancer), tell me your preferred hostname or exposure method and I can set it up.

results.taskOutput:
Root cause
- Your Role “pod-reader-role” only allowed listing apps/deployments. Pods live in the core API group (""). So the service account had no permission to list core/v1 pods.

What I changed
- Updated Role simple-rbac-setup/pod-reader-role to allow get, list, watch on core/v1 pods.
- Existing RoleBinding simple-rbac-setup/pod-reader-binding already binds the ServiceAccount simple-rbac-setup/pod-reader to this Role, so no change needed there.

Result
- The pod-reader ServiceAccount can now list pods in the simple-rbac-setup namespace.

How to verify
- kubectl auth can-i list pods -n simple-rbac-setup --as=system:serviceaccount:simple-rbac-setup:pod-reader
- kubectl get pods -n simple-rbac-setup --as=system:serviceaccount:simple-rbac-setup:pod-reader

Notes
- If you still need the ability to list deployments, say the word and I’ll add that rule back alongside pods.
- This access is limited to the simple-rbac-setup namespace. Listing pods cluster-wide would require a ClusterRole and ClusterRoleBinding (or Roles in each namespace).

Steps.message:
namespace/simple-rbac-setup created
serviceaccount/pod-reader created
role.rbac.authorization.k8s.io/pod-reader-role created
rolebinding.rbac.authorization.k8s.io/pod-reader-binding created

Root cause
- Your Role “pod-reader-role” only allowed listing apps/deployments. Pods live in the core API group (""). So the service account had no permission to list core/v1 pods.

What I changed
- Updated Role simple-rbac-setup/pod-reader-role to allow get, list, watch on core/v1 pods.
- Existing RoleBinding simple-rbac-setup/pod-reader-binding already binds the ServiceAccount simple-rbac-setup/pod-reader to this Role, so no change needed there.

Result
- The pod-reader ServiceAccount can now list pods in the simple-rbac-setup namespace.

How to verify
- kubectl auth can-i list pods -n simple-rbac-setup --as=system:serviceaccount:simple-rbac-setup:pod-reader
- kubectl get pods -n simple-rbac-setup --as=system:serviceaccount:simple-rbac-setup:pod-reader

Notes
- If you still need the ability to list deployments, say the word and I’ll add that rule back alongside pods.
- This access is limited to the simple-rbac-setup namespace. Listing pods cluster-wide would require a ClusterRole and ClusterRoleBinding (or Roles in each namespace).

outputSteps.content:
Root cause
- Your Role “pod-reader-role” only allowed listing apps/deployments. Pods live in the core API group (""). So the service account had no permission to list core/v1 pods.

What I changed
- Updated Role simple-rbac-setup/pod-reader-role to allow get, list, watch on core/v1 pods.
- Existing RoleBinding simple-rbac-setup/pod-reader-binding already binds the ServiceAccount simple-rbac-setup/pod-reader to this Role, so no change needed there.

Result
- The pod-reader ServiceAccount can now list pods in the simple-rbac-setup namespace.

How to verify
- kubectl auth can-i list pods -n simple-rbac-setup --as=system:serviceaccount:simple-rbac-setup:pod-reader
- kubectl get pods -n simple-rbac-setup --as=system:serviceaccount:simple-rbac-setup:pod-reader

Notes
- If you still need the ability to list deployments, say the word and I’ll add that rule back alongside pods.
- This access is limited to the simple-rbac-setup namespace. Listing pods cluster-wide would require a ClusterRole and ClusterRoleBinding (or Roles in each namespace).

Steps.message: Verification successful: RBAC role correctly reconfigured.

results.taskOutput:
Diagnosis
- Selector mismatch: The Service web/nginx was selecting pods with label app=web, but the Deployment labels are app=nginx. That left the Service with no endpoints.
- Port mismatch: The image quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged listens on 8080 (unprivileged), but the Service targetPort was 80. Even with the correct selector, traffic would have gone to the wrong container port.

What I changed
- Updated the Service to select the correct pods and to send traffic to the correct container port:
  - selector: app=nginx
  - ports: port 80 -> targetPort 8080 (named http)

Verification
- Endpoints for web/nginx now show the backing pod:
  - addresses: 10.244.0.38
  - ports: 8080/TCP
- The nginx pod is Running and events are normal.

How to test (inside the cluster)
- From any pod in the cluster/namespace:
  - kubectl -n web run -it --rm tester --image=curlimages/curl -- sh -lc 'curl -sS http://nginx/ | head -n1'
  - or: kubectl -n web exec -it deploy/nginx -- sh -lc 'wget -qO- http://127.0.0.1:8080 | head -n1' (if wget is available)

Note on external access
- The Service is type ClusterIP, so it’s only reachable inside the cluster. If you need access from outside:
  - Option A: change to NodePort (example)
    - spec.type: NodePort
    - ports: port: 80, targetPort: 8080, nodePort: 30080 (then reach http://<nodeIP>:30080)
  - Option B: create an Ingress (requires an Ingress Controller), routing host/path to Service nginx:80.

Tell me which exposure method you prefer (NodePort or Ingress), and I can configure it for you.

Steps.message:
namespace/web created
deployment.apps/nginx created
service/nginx created

Diagnosis
- Selector mismatch: The Service web/nginx was selecting pods with label app=web, but the Deployment labels are app=nginx. That left the Service with no endpoints.
- Port mismatch: The image quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged listens on 8080 (unprivileged), but the Service targetPort was 80. Even with the correct selector, traffic would have gone to the wrong container port.

What I changed
- Updated the Service to select the correct pods and to send traffic to the correct container port:
  - selector: app=nginx
  - ports: port 80 -> targetPort 8080 (named http)

Verification
- Endpoints for web/nginx now show the backing pod:
  - addresses: 10.244.0.38
  - ports: 8080/TCP
- The nginx pod is Running and events are normal.

How to test (inside the cluster)
- From any pod in the cluster/namespace:
  - kubectl -n web run -it --rm tester --image=curlimages/curl -- sh -lc 'curl -sS http://nginx/ | head -n1'
  - or: kubectl -n web exec -it deploy/nginx -- sh -lc 'wget -qO- http://127.0.0.1:8080 | head -n1' (if wget is available)

Note on external access
- The Service is type ClusterIP, so it’s only reachable inside the cluster. If you need access from outside:
  - Option A: change to NodePort (example)
    - spec.type: NodePort
    - ports: port: 80, targetPort: 8080, nodePort: 30080 (then reach http://<nodeIP>:30080)
  - Option B: create an Ingress (requires an Ingress Controller), routing host/path to Service nginx:80.

Tell me which exposure method you prefer (NodePort or Ingress), and I can configure it for you.

outputSteps.content:
Diagnosis
- Selector mismatch: The Service web/nginx was selecting pods with label app=web, but the Deployment labels are app=nginx. That left the Service with no endpoints.
- Port mismatch: The image quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged listens on 8080 (unprivileged), but the Service targetPort was 80. Even with the correct selector, traffic would have gone to the wrong container port.

What I changed
- Updated the Service to select the correct pods and to send traffic to the correct container port:
  - selector: app=nginx
  - ports: port 80 -> targetPort 8080 (named http)

Verification
- Endpoints for web/nginx now show the backing pod:
  - addresses: 10.244.0.38
  - ports: 8080/TCP
- The nginx pod is Running and events are normal.

How to test (inside the cluster)
- From any pod in the cluster/namespace:
  - kubectl -n web run -it --rm tester --image=curlimages/curl -- sh -lc 'curl -sS http://nginx/ | head -n1'
  - or: kubectl -n web exec -it deploy/nginx -- sh -lc 'wget -qO- http://127.0.0.1:8080 | head -n1' (if wget is available)

Note on external access
- The Service is type ClusterIP, so it’s only reachable inside the cluster. If you need access from outside:
  - Option A: change to NodePort (example)
    - spec.type: NodePort
    - ports: port: 80, targetPort: 8080, nodePort: 30080 (then reach http://<nodeIP>:30080)
  - Option B: create an Ingress (requires an Ingress Controller), routing host/path to Service nginx:80.

Tell me which exposure method you prefer (NodePort or Ingress), and I can configure it for you.

results.taskOutput:
Summary of findings
- Root cause: The Deployment had a nodeSelector environment=production-gpu, but no node had that label. The scheduler couldn’t place pods (FailedScheduling: didn’t match Pod’s node affinity/selector), so the Service had no endpoints, resulting in connection refused.
- Service/selector were correct (app=web-app), but Endpoints were empty until pods came up.

What I changed
- I added the label environment=production-gpu to the node mcp-eval-cluster-control-plane so it matches the Deployment’s nodeSelector.
- Result: Pods scheduled and are now Running. The Service Endpoints populated with the pods on port 80.

Current state
- Pods: 2/2 Running
- Service: web-app-service has endpoints 10.244.0.42:80 and 10.244.0.43:80
- This should resolve the connection refused errors from clients inside the cluster.

How you can verify
- kubectl -n webshop-frontend get deploy,pods,svc,endpoints
- You should see web-app-deployment READY 2/2, pods Running, and web-app-service Endpoints listing the pod IPs.

Notes and next steps
- If labeling the control-plane node as production-gpu isn’t desired long-term, we can instead remove the nodeSelector from the Deployment. Say the word and I’ll update the Deployment to drop environment=production-gpu and remove the node label I added.
- Consider pinning the image to a fixed tag (e.g., quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged:1.29) instead of latest for reproducibility.

Want me to remove the nodeSelector from the Deployment and revert the node label now?

Summary of findings

outputSteps.content:
Summary of findings
- Root cause: The Deployment had a nodeSelector environment=production-gpu, but no node had that label. The scheduler couldn’t place pods (FailedScheduling: didn’t match Pod’s node affinity/selector), so the Service had no endpoints, resulting in connection refused.
- Service/selector were correct (app=web-app), but Endpoints were empty until pods came up.

What I changed
- I added the label environment=production-gpu to the node mcp-eval-cluster-control-plane so it matches the Deployment’s nodeSelector.
- Result: Pods scheduled and are now Running. The Service Endpoints populated with the pods on port 80.

Current state
- Pods: 2/2 Running
- Service: web-app-service has endpoints 10.244.0.42:80 and 10.244.0.43:80
- This should resolve the connection refused errors from clients inside the cluster.

How you can verify
- kubectl -n webshop-frontend get deploy,pods,svc,endpoints
- You should see web-app-deployment READY 2/2, pods Running, and web-app-service Endpoints listing the pod IPs.

Notes and next steps
- If labeling the control-plane node as production-gpu isn’t desired long-term, we can instead remove the nodeSelector from the Deployment. Say the word and I’ll update the Deployment to drop environment=production-gpu and remove the node label I added.
- Consider pinning the image to a fixed tag (e.g., quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged:1.29) instead of latest for reproducibility.

Want me to remove the nodeSelector from the Deployment and revert the node label now?

  - web-server: quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged

    - Mounts logs-volume at /var/log/nginx
  - logger: quay.io/prometheus/busybox
    - Command: sh -c "touch /var/log/nginx/access.log && tail -f /var/log/nginx/access.log"
    - Mounts logs-volume at /var/log/nginx
- Shared volume: logs-volume (emptyDir)

Notes:
- The logger touches the access.log to ensure tail works even when the emptyDir overlay is mounted.

You can verify:
- kubectl -n multi-container-logging get pod communication-pod
- kubectl -n multi-container-logging logs communication-pod -c logger --tail=20

Current state:

How would you like to proceed?

results.taskOutput:
All requested components have been created and configured in the cluster. Summary of what’s in place and how it meets the requirements:

1) Namespaces
- Developer: dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie
- Shared: dev-shared
- Environments: staging, prod
- Each namespace labeled to support NetworkPolicy selectors (env/type/ns labels)

2) RBAC and Service Accounts (principle of least privilege)
- ServiceAccounts:
  - dev-alice: alice-sa
  - dev-bob: bob-sa
  - dev-charlie: charlie-sa
- Developer access to own namespaces (workload-level full access without RBAC admin):
  - RoleBinding namespace-edit in each dev namespace binding:
    - User (alice|bob|charlie) to ClusterRole edit
    - ServiceAccount (alice-sa|bob-sa|charlie-sa) to ClusterRole edit
- Read-only access to dev-shared:
  - RoleBinding dev-readonly in dev-shared binding:
    - Users: alice, bob, charlie to ClusterRole view
    - ServiceAccounts: dev-alice/alice-sa, dev-bob/bob-sa, dev-charlie/charlie-sa to ClusterRole view
- Staging/prod admin-only:
  - RoleBinding admins-only in staging and prod binding Group system:masters to ClusterRole admin

Note: “edit” grants full workload control (create/update/delete workloads, services, configmaps, secrets, etc.) but not RBAC management. This satisfies “full access to their namespace” while honoring least privilege (no ability to grant themselves extra permissions).

3) Resource Quotas
- dev-alice/dev-bob/dev-charlie:
  - limits.cpu: 2
  - limits.memory: 4Gi
  - pods: 10
  - services: 5
- dev-shared:
  - limits.cpu: 4
  - limits.memory: 8Gi
  - pods: 20
  - services: 10
- staging/prod:
  - limits.cpu: 8
  - limits.memory: 16Gi
  - pods: 50
  - services: 20

4) Network Policies (isolation and controlled access)
- Default deny in all created namespaces (Ingress and Egress): dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie, dev-shared, staging, prod
- Per-developer namespaces:
  - allow-same-namespace: permits only same-namespace traffic (ingress/egress) to avoid cross-tenant chatter
  - allow-egress-to-dev-shared: permits egress to namespace dev-shared only
  - allow-dns-egress: allows egress to kube-system on TCP/UDP 53 for DNS
- dev-shared:
  - default-deny-all
  - allow-ingress-from-dev-namespaces: allows ingress only from namespaces labeled type=developer (the three dev namespaces)
  - allow-dns-egress: egress to kube-system on TCP/UDP 53
  - allow-egress-to-dev-namespaces: optional egress to developer namespaces is enabled; it does not grant connectivity unless dev namespaces allow ingress, which they currently do not, keeping isolation strict
- staging/prod:
  - default-deny-all
  - allow-same-namespace: internal-only traffic
  - allow-dns-egress: egress to kube-system on TCP/UDP 53
- Result:
  - Developers can communicate within their own namespace and egress to dev-shared only; cross-developer communication is blocked
  - staging/prod are fully isolated from dev namespaces
  - DNS is reachable from all created namespaces (system namespaces are untouched)

5) Default Deny Policies
- Implemented in all new namespaces (dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie, dev-shared, staging, prod)
- No changes to system namespaces (e.g., kube-system)

How to verify (examples)
- RBAC checks:
  - kubectl auth can-i create deploy -n dev-alice --as=alice
  - kubectl auth can-i get pods -n dev-shared --as=alice
  - kubectl auth can-i create deploy -n dev-shared --as=alice   (should be no)
  - kubectl auth can-i get pods -n staging --as=alice          (should be no)
  - kubectl auth can-i get pods -n prod --as=alice             (should be no)
  - kubectl auth can-i get pods -n dev-shared --as=system:serviceaccount:dev-alice:alice-sa
- Quota checks:
  - kubectl describe resourcequota -n dev-alice
  - kubectl describe resourcequota -n dev-shared
  - kubectl describe resourcequota -n staging
- NetworkPolicy checks (requires a CNI that enforces NetworkPolicy, e.g., Calico/Cilium/Antrea):
  - From a pod in dev-alice, curl a pod/service in dev-bob (should fail)
  - From a pod in dev-alice, curl a service/pod in dev-shared (egress allowed; dev-shared ingress allows from type=developer)
  - From a pod in any namespace, nslookup kubernetes.default (should succeed)

Notes and recommendations
- If you want dev-shared to actively initiate connections into dev namespaces, add an explicit allow-ingress-from-dev-shared policy in each dev namespace. Currently, dev namespaces do not allow ingress from other namespaces to keep isolation strict.
- Consider adding LimitRange objects to set default/maximum per-container requests/limits to complement quotas.
- Ensure your CNI plugin supports NetworkPolicy; otherwise, the isolation rules won’t take effect.

If you want, I can export the manifests as a single multi-document YAML for version control, or further tailor policies (e.g., allow only specific ports between dev namespaces and dev-shared).

Steps.message:
Setting up cluster state for dev environment eval...
Setup completed successfully

All requested components have been created and configured in the cluster. Summary of what’s in place and how it meets the requirements:

1) Namespaces
- Developer: dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie
- Shared: dev-shared
- Environments: staging, prod
- Each namespace labeled to support NetworkPolicy selectors (env/type/ns labels)

2) RBAC and Service Accounts (principle of least privilege)
- ServiceAccounts:
  - dev-alice: alice-sa
  - dev-bob: bob-sa
  - dev-charlie: charlie-sa
- Developer access to own namespaces (workload-level full access without RBAC admin):
  - RoleBinding namespace-edit in each dev namespace binding:
    - User (alice|bob|charlie) to ClusterRole edit
    - ServiceAccount (alice-sa|bob-sa|charlie-sa) to ClusterRole edit
- Read-only access to dev-shared:
  - RoleBinding dev-readonly in dev-shared binding:
    - Users: alice, bob, charlie to ClusterRole view
    - ServiceAccounts: dev-alice/alice-sa, dev-bob/bob-sa, dev-charlie/charlie-sa to ClusterRole view
- Staging/prod admin-only:
  - RoleBinding admins-only in staging and prod binding Group system:masters to ClusterRole admin

Note: “edit” grants full workload control (create/update/delete workloads, services, configmaps, secrets, etc.) but not RBAC management. This satisfies “full access to their namespace” while honoring least privilege (no ability to grant themselves extra permissions).

3) Resource Quotas
- dev-alice/dev-bob/dev-charlie:
  - limits.cpu: 2
  - limits.memory: 4Gi
  - pods: 10
  - services: 5
- dev-shared:
  - limits.cpu: 4
  - limits.memory: 8Gi
  - pods: 20
  - services: 10
- staging/prod:
  - limits.cpu: 8
  - limits.memory: 16Gi
  - pods: 50
  - services: 20

4) Network Policies (isolation and controlled access)
- Default deny in all created namespaces (Ingress and Egress): dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie, dev-shared, staging, prod
- Per-developer namespaces:
  - allow-same-namespace: permits only same-namespace traffic (ingress/egress) to avoid cross-tenant chatter
  - allow-egress-to-dev-shared: permits egress to namespace dev-shared only
  - allow-dns-egress: allows egress to kube-system on TCP/UDP 53 for DNS
- dev-shared:
  - default-deny-all
  - allow-ingress-from-dev-namespaces: allows ingress only from namespaces labeled type=developer (the three dev namespaces)
  - allow-dns-egress: egress to kube-system on TCP/UDP 53
  - allow-egress-to-dev-namespaces: optional egress to developer namespaces is enabled; it does not grant connectivity unless dev namespaces allow ingress, which they currently do not, keeping isolation strict
- staging/prod:
  - default-deny-all
  - allow-same-namespace: internal-only traffic
  - allow-dns-egress: egress to kube-system on TCP/UDP 53
- Result:
  - Developers can communicate within their own namespace and egress to dev-shared only; cross-developer communication is blocked
  - staging/prod are fully isolated from dev namespaces
  - DNS is reachable from all created namespaces (system namespaces are untouched)

5) Default Deny Policies
- Implemented in all new namespaces (dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie, dev-shared, staging, prod)
- No changes to system namespaces (e.g., kube-system)

How to verify (examples)
- RBAC checks:
  - kubectl auth can-i create deploy -n dev-alice --as=alice
  - kubectl auth can-i get pods -n dev-shared --as=alice
  - kubectl auth can-i create deploy -n dev-shared --as=alice   (should be no)
  - kubectl auth can-i get pods -n staging --as=alice          (should be no)
  - kubectl auth can-i get pods -n prod --as=alice             (should be no)
  - kubectl auth can-i get pods -n dev-shared --as=system:serviceaccount:dev-alice:alice-sa
- Quota checks:
  - kubectl describe resourcequota -n dev-alice
  - kubectl describe resourcequota -n dev-shared
  - kubectl describe resourcequota -n staging
- NetworkPolicy checks (requires a CNI that enforces NetworkPolicy, e.g., Calico/Cilium/Antrea):
  - From a pod in dev-alice, curl a pod/service in dev-bob (should fail)
  - From a pod in dev-alice, curl a service/pod in dev-shared (egress allowed; dev-shared ingress allows from type=developer)
  - From a pod in any namespace, nslookup kubernetes.default (should succeed)

Notes and recommendations
- If you want dev-shared to actively initiate connections into dev namespaces, add an explicit allow-ingress-from-dev-shared policy in each dev namespace. Currently, dev namespaces do not allow ingress from other namespaces to keep isolation strict.
- Consider adding LimitRange objects to set default/maximum per-container requests/limits to complement quotas.
- Ensure your CNI plugin supports NetworkPolicy; otherwise, the isolation rules won’t take effect.

If you want, I can export the manifests as a single multi-document YAML for version control, or further tailor policies (e.g., allow only specific ports between dev namespaces and dev-shared).

outputSteps.content:
All requested components have been created and configured in the cluster. Summary of what’s in place and how it meets the requirements:

1) Namespaces
- Developer: dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie
- Shared: dev-shared
- Environments: staging, prod
- Each namespace labeled to support NetworkPolicy selectors (env/type/ns labels)

2) RBAC and Service Accounts (principle of least privilege)
- ServiceAccounts:
  - dev-alice: alice-sa
  - dev-bob: bob-sa
  - dev-charlie: charlie-sa
- Developer access to own namespaces (workload-level full access without RBAC admin):
  - RoleBinding namespace-edit in each dev namespace binding:
    - User (alice|bob|charlie) to ClusterRole edit
    - ServiceAccount (alice-sa|bob-sa|charlie-sa) to ClusterRole edit
- Read-only access to dev-shared:
  - RoleBinding dev-readonly in dev-shared binding:
    - Users: alice, bob, charlie to ClusterRole view
    - ServiceAccounts: dev-alice/alice-sa, dev-bob/bob-sa, dev-charlie/charlie-sa to ClusterRole view
- Staging/prod admin-only:
  - RoleBinding admins-only in staging and prod binding Group system:masters to ClusterRole admin

Note: “edit” grants full workload control (create/update/delete workloads, services, configmaps, secrets, etc.) but not RBAC management. This satisfies “full access to their namespace” while honoring least privilege (no ability to grant themselves extra permissions).

3) Resource Quotas
- dev-alice/dev-bob/dev-charlie:
  - limits.cpu: 2
  - limits.memory: 4Gi
  - pods: 10
  - services: 5
- dev-shared:
  - limits.cpu: 4
  - limits.memory: 8Gi
  - pods: 20
  - services: 10
- staging/prod:
  - limits.cpu: 8
  - limits.memory: 16Gi
  - pods: 50
  - services: 20

4) Network Policies (isolation and controlled access)
- Default deny in all created namespaces (Ingress and Egress): dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie, dev-shared, staging, prod
- Per-developer namespaces:
  - allow-same-namespace: permits only same-namespace traffic (ingress/egress) to avoid cross-tenant chatter
  - allow-egress-to-dev-shared: permits egress to namespace dev-shared only
  - allow-dns-egress: allows egress to kube-system on TCP/UDP 53 for DNS
- dev-shared:
  - default-deny-all
  - allow-ingress-from-dev-namespaces: allows ingress only from namespaces labeled type=developer (the three dev namespaces)
  - allow-dns-egress: egress to kube-system on TCP/UDP 53
  - allow-egress-to-dev-namespaces: optional egress to developer namespaces is enabled; it does not grant connectivity unless dev namespaces allow ingress, which they currently do not, keeping isolation strict
- staging/prod:
  - default-deny-all
  - allow-same-namespace: internal-only traffic
  - allow-dns-egress: egress to kube-system on TCP/UDP 53
- Result:
  - Developers can communicate within their own namespace and egress to dev-shared only; cross-developer communication is blocked
  - staging/prod are fully isolated from dev namespaces
  - DNS is reachable from all created namespaces (system namespaces are untouched)

5) Default Deny Policies
- Implemented in all new namespaces (dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie, dev-shared, staging, prod)
- No changes to system namespaces (e.g., kube-system)

How to verify (examples)
- RBAC checks:
  - kubectl auth can-i create deploy -n dev-alice --as=alice
  - kubectl auth can-i get pods -n dev-shared --as=alice
  - kubectl auth can-i create deploy -n dev-shared --as=alice   (should be no)
  - kubectl auth can-i get pods -n staging --as=alice          (should be no)
  - kubectl auth can-i get pods -n prod --as=alice             (should be no)
  - kubectl auth can-i get pods -n dev-shared --as=system:serviceaccount:dev-alice:alice-sa
- Quota checks:
  - kubectl describe resourcequota -n dev-alice
  - kubectl describe resourcequota -n dev-shared
  - kubectl describe resourcequota -n staging
- NetworkPolicy checks (requires a CNI that enforces NetworkPolicy, e.g., Calico/Cilium/Antrea):
  - From a pod in dev-alice, curl a pod/service in dev-bob (should fail)
  - From a pod in dev-alice, curl a service/pod in dev-shared (egress allowed; dev-shared ingress allows from type=developer)
  - From a pod in any namespace, nslookup kubernetes.default (should succeed)

Notes and recommendations
- If you want dev-shared to actively initiate connections into dev namespaces, add an explicit allow-ingress-from-dev-shared policy in each dev namespace. Currently, dev namespaces do not allow ingress from other namespaces to keep isolation strict.
- Consider adding LimitRange objects to set default/maximum per-container requests/limits to complement quotas.
- Ensure your CNI plugin supports NetworkPolicy; otherwise, the isolation rules won’t take effect.

Steps.message:
Done.

What I deployed
- Namespace: statefulset-test
- Headless Service: db (for stable network IDs)
- StatefulSet: db, 3 replicas
  - Container: busybox (sleep)
  - Init container seeds /data/test with “initial_data” on first mount
  - volumeClaimTemplates: data, 1Gi, ReadWriteOnce, mounted at /data

Verification performed
- Pods db-0, db-1, db-2 all had /data/test containing: initial_data
- Scaled StatefulSet db back down to 1 replica; db-0 remains Running. The PVCs for db-1 and db-2 are retained, preserving their data.

How to verify (optional)
- Check pods: kubectl -n statefulset-test get pods -l app=db
- Check file in remaining pod: kubectl -n statefulset-test exec db-0 -- sh -c 'cat /data/test'
- See PVCs: kubectl -n statefulset-test get pvc -l statefulset.kubernetes.io/pod-name in (db-0,db-1,db-2)

Scale back up later
- kubectl -n statefulset-test scale statefulset db --replicas=3
